Q: What activities am I supposed to be doing and when?


A: Try to do one or two Microdoses (also called “sessions”) each day. You can do them at any time. Every other week, you will also be asked to fill out a 20-minute survey.


Q: Why am I filling in letters?


A:We want you to learn that situations can turn out in many different ways. The endings, where letters are missing, are the most important part of the training. That’s when your brain gets a chance to see a situation end differently than it expected. Research suggests that filling in the missing letters, instead of just reading the words, may make the program work better.


Q: Why are some of the stories repetitive?


A: The app is designed to help you build a new skill: thinking “flexibly.” Like any skill, it takes practice. Changing our thinking habits takes time, so please be patient and stick with it! To learn more, see Program Rationale on the app’s home page


Q: Why do some stories have a negative ending?


A: In real life, the worst does happen sometimes! The purpose of the training sessions is to encourage flexible thinking, or the ability to switch between positive, negative, and neutral thoughts. As you practice, you will learn that there are many different ways a situation can turn out, and the worst-case scenario is only one of them. To learn more, please see Program Rationale, accessible from the app's home page.


Q: When the app is open, is it draining my phone battery?


A: The app has minimal impact on battery use because it does not collect data when it is not being actively used.


Q: How is my data being protected?


A: Your data is encrypted, which means it is scrambled so others can’t read it. It also does not include your name or anything else that could identify you. Your data is saved on your phone for a short time. Then it is sent to secure storage in Azure. This happens right after you finish a session, as long as you have WiFi or cellular data. When the study ends, the data is moved from Amazon Cloud to an encrypted hard drive. Only the research team can see your data.


Q: Who should I contact if I'm having technical difficulties?


A: You can contact rpu3zk@virginia.edu if you are experiencing any technical issues. For best assistance, please include the following information in your email:

  • What device are you using (e.g., iPhone, Android phone)?
  • What operating system version are you using (e.g., iOS 26.6.1)?
  • What app version do you have (e.g., 1.9.8)?


Q: What is CBM-I?


A: CBM-I stands for cognitive bias modification for interpretations. People with anxiety tend to have unhelpful thinking patterns. CBM-I can change these patterns. For example, when someone with anxiety is meeting someone new, they might quickly jump to the conclusion that the person doesn't like them. CBM-I provides a chance to repeatedly practice thinking in new ways to try to undo that tendency to assume the worst. This builds "flexible" thinking skills. Instead of immediately assuming the worst outcome, users are encouraged to think about different possibilities, and imagine other, less bad ways that uncertain situations might turn out. Each session that you complete in the app provides a brief dose of CBM-I, which involves reading a story and thinking flexibly about how the story ends. The goal is that, with lots of practice with different stories in the app, your brain will develop a habit of flexible thinking. We hope you can then use that flexible thinking skill when uncertain situations come up in your everyday life. Research shows that CBM-I can reduce negative thought patterns and anxiety for many people, and can increase positive thinking.


Q: When answering questions (following each of the brief stories), the program keeps telling me that my answer is incorrect. Why?


A: A: This is because we are specifically looking for the answer that is consistent with the information given to you in the stories. This answer might be different from how you would typically answer in a given situation, but our goal is to immerse you in the story as we describe the beginning, middle, and end. The training will work best if you fully immerse yourself in each story, exactly as it is described.


Q: When trying to complete word fragments at the end of the brief stories, the program keeps telling me my answer is incorrect. Why?


A: Please complete the word fragments based only on information given to you in the brief stories. The resulting word may represent a different ending to the story than you would typically imagine, and that’s the point! Repeated practice thinking in this new way builds flexible thinking skills, which have been shown to reduce anxiety.


Q: How can I get more help for my stress and anxiety?


A: Our team has put together a list of resources with more information on anxiety and mental health treatment. Please see Resources, accessible from the app's home page. In case of emergencies, you can contact the following:


Phone Hotlines


Emergency Services: 911


Dial 911 or visit the emergency department of your local hospital.


National Suicide Prevention Lifeline: 988


Calls are automatically directed to the nearest local Crisis Center in the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline network and answered by trained crisis counselors. Available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.



Text Hotlines


Crisis Text Line: Text HOME to 741741


Have a text conversation with a volunteer crisis counselor. Free, 24/7 support in the US. More info at Crisis Text Line.


The Trevor Project Hotline: 1-866-488-7386


Staffed by trained counselors and provides support to LBGTQ+ teens. Available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.



Hotlines for Speech-Impaired and Deaf Callers


National Suicide Prevention Lifeline (TTY): Use your preferred relay service or dial 711 then 988. Available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.



Suicide Prevention Websites


National Suicide Prevention Lifeline: National Suicide Prevention Lifeline: Provides a search for the nearest crisis center in the Lifeline Network and information for Veterans and their families.


Suicide.org: Provides resources for helping a loved one who is suicidal and a list of suicide hotlines outside of the U.S.


SuicideHotlines.com: Provides information on what to expect when calling a hotline and a directory of local hotlines by state.
